title: Normalized graph image as an intermediate valuation-curve model
statement:
Let $K$ be a separably closed [def-kun-separably-closed] field [def-weil-field] and $V\subset K$ a valuation ring with fraction field $K$: for every $a\in K^	imes$, either $a$ or $a^{-1}$ lies in $V$. Assume that the prime ideals of $V$ form a finite chain, and put $T=\operatorname{Spec}V$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], with generic point $\eta=\operatorname{Spec}K$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be normal $T$-curves with smooth generic fibres, let $f:Y	o X$ be an $\eta$-modification, and let $u:Y	o\mathbf P^1_T$ be any $T$-morphism [def-nagata-projective-space-base-change]. Let $I$ be the scheme-theoretic image of $(f,u):Y	o\mathbf P^1_X$, namely the closed subscheme whose ideal is the kernel of $\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^1_X}	o(f,u)_*\mathcal O_Y$. Let $H$ be the normalization of $I$ in the product of the function fields of its components. Then $I$ is a reduced $T$-curve, $H	o I$ is finite, and $H$ is a normal $T$-curve. Write $
u:H	o I$ for the normalization morphism and $p:I	o X$ for the projection. The graph map $h=(f,u):Y	o I$ has a unique factorization $h=
u q$ with $q:Y	o H$. Put $g=p
u:H	o X$; both $q$ and $g$ are $\eta$-modifications and $gq=f$. Every geometric fibre of $q$ is connected. A fibre component $A$ of $Y$ is contracted by $q$ if and only if both $f|_A$ and $u|_A$ have zero-dimensional image. The modification locus of $q$ consists exactly of points with positive-dimensional fibre. In particular, $q$ is an isomorphism over each open of $X$ on which $f$ is an isomorphism. A component is contracted when its image has dimension zero; all assertions refer to the reduced underlying components. A $T$-curve means a flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] $T$-scheme of pure relative dimension one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. A geometric fibre is the base change of a fibre to an algebraic closure of its residue field [def-weil-geometric-fibre]; geometrically reduced means all such fibres have no nonzero nilpotents. An $\eta$-modification is a proper morphism [def-weil-proper-morphism] which is an isomorphism over the generic fibre and over schematically dense open subschemes; schematic density means injectivity of $\mathcal O_Z	o j_*\mathcal O_U$ for the open inclusion. A scheme is normal if every local ring is an integrally closed domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]. Its normalization means the scheme obtained by taking the integral closure of its structure sheaf in the product of the function fields of its irreducible components; for an integral scheme this is [def-sc-normalization].

source.place: Proof of Proposition 4.4.6, printed p. 33, normalization of the relative P1-image; Lemma 4.4.1(i), printed p. 30, and the normal-target connectedness and finite-modification argument of Lemmas 4.4.2 and 4.2.1; primary PDF read online; local archival copy WANTED (report.md).

proof.text: The generic point is a retrocompact schematically dense open in $T$. If $V$ is a field use $a=1$; otherwise choose nonzero $a$ in the least nonzero prime. All nonzero primes contain $a$, so $D(a)=\eta$ and $V[1/a]=K$. For any open $W$ in a flat $T$-scheme, [lem-sc-flat-invertible-sections-torsion-free], with the invertible module $\mathcal O_W$, makes multiplication by every nonzero element of $V$ injective on $\Gamma(W,\mathcal O_W)$. On affine opens localization at $a$ is therefore injective. Thus the generic fibre is schematically dense in every flat $T$-scheme used below, also when it is empty.

source.place: Tag 0539, torsion-freeness of flat modules; finite-height principal generic open (agent calculation)

proof.text: Put $P=\mathbf P^1_X$, $\pi:P\to X$ and $\widetilde h=(f,u):Y\to P$. The projective-space properness node makes $\pi$ proper, hence separated. By [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated] over $X$, $\widetilde h$ is proper because its source has proper structure map $f$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-theoretic-image-proper] with base $X$, source $Y$, and target $P$. It gives the scheme-theoretic image $i:I\hookrightarrow P$, a surjection $h:Y\to I$, and properness of $p=\pi i:I\to X$. Applying proper-to-separated once more, with target the separated $X$-scheme $I$, makes $h$ proper. In particular $I\to T$ is finite type by properness of $p$, finite presentation of $X\to T$, and finite-type composition.

source.place: Tags 01W6 (proper source to separated target), 0AH6 (proper scheme-theoretic image), 01T3 (composition)

proof.text: On an affine open $W=\operatorname{Spec}B\subset P$, let $J=\ker(B\to\Gamma(\widetilde h^{-1}W,\mathcal O_Y))$. The scheme-image kernel statement identifies $I\cap W$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(B/J)$. Since $Y$ is normal, its sections are reduced: a nilpotent section has zero germ at every point. Hence $B/J$, a subring of those sections, is reduced. By step 1 the section module on $\widetilde h^{-1}W$ is torsion-free over $V$, so its submodule $B/J$ is torsion-free as well. [lem-trf-valuation-torsionfree-flat] makes $B/J$ flat over $V$, and the affine flatness criterion makes $I\to T$ flat.

Apply scheme-image restriction to the open $P_\eta\subset P$. Since $f_\eta$ is an isomorphism, $\widetilde h_\eta$ is the graph of the morphism $u_\eta$ on $X_\eta$, a closed immersion because projective space is separated. The kernel ideal of a closed immersion gives its source as its scheme-theoretic image. Consequently $I_\eta\simeq Y_\eta\simeq X_\eta$, and $h_\eta$ and $p_\eta$ are isomorphisms. In particular $I_\eta$ is smooth and pure of dimension one. Its schematic density follows from step 3 and step 1.

source.place: Tag 01R8 (restriction of scheme-theoretic image); graph of a morphism into a separated scheme

proof.text: Finite presentation of $I\to T$ needs an additional argument: a closed immersion into a finitely presented scheme need not be finitely presented. The standard projective charts show that $P\to T$ is locally of finite presentation: over each affine chart of $X$ its rings are polynomial algebras in one variable. Regard $i_*\mathcal O_I$ as a finite-type quasi-coherent $\mathcal O_P$-module (locally it is the cyclic module $B/J$). It is $T$-flat by step 3. Its generic restriction is finitely presented: $P_\eta$ is finite type over a field, hence Noetherian, and finite modules over a Noetherian ring are finitely presented. Apply [lem-trf-flat-finite-type-dense-presentation] to $P\to T$, this module, and the retrocompact dense open $\eta$ of step 1. Thus $B/J$ is finitely presented as a $B$-module. The kernel $J$ of the surjection $B\to B/J$ is therefore finitely generated, so the closed immersion $i$ is locally of finite presentation. Composing with $P\to T$ proves local finite presentation of $I\to T$. The global quasi-compact and quasi-separated conditions hold because $p$ is proper and $X\to T$ is finitely presented; the qcqs permanence node gives them for $I\to T$. Hence $I\to T$ is finitely presented.

source.place: Tag 081N (lemma-flat-finite-type-finitely-presented-over-dense-open); Morphisms Tag 01TP (definition of finite presentation)

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-flat-dense-generic-fibre-pure-dimension] to the flat finite-type morphism $I\to T$. The base $T$ is integral, step 1 gives the dense generic fibre, and step 4 gives its pure dimension one. Thus all nonempty fibres of $I$ are pure one-dimensional. Together with reducedness, flatness and finite presentation from steps 3 and 5, this proves that $I$ is a reduced $T$-curve. Steps 1 and 4 also show that the proper map $h:Y\to I$ is an $\eta$-modification: its generic-fibre isomorphism identifies schematically dense opens on source and target.

source.place: Tag 0GSK (remark-flat-equidimensional); Temkin Lemma 3.5.1 and the last paragraph of the proof of Proposition 4.4.6

proof.text:
Apply [lem-trf-valuation-curve-projective-preparation] to the $T$-curve $I$, whose generic fibre is smooth by step 4. Its stated normalization assertion gives the finite $\eta$-modification $
u:H	o I$ and says that $H$ is a normal $T$-curve with geometrically reduced fibres. Since the source $Y$ of the $\eta$-modification $h$ is normal, the factorization assertion of that same node gives a unique $q:Y	o H$ with $
u q=h$. Define $g=p
u:H	o X$. This establishes the normalization construction and fixes the two different codomains: $
u$ ends in $I$, while $g$ ends in $X$. The equation $gq=ph=f$ follows by composition.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.1(i), printed p. 30; normalization factorization; last paragraph of Proposition 4.4.6 proof, printed p. 33

proof.text:
Since $
u$ is finite and $p$ proper, [lem-weil-pbc-finite-morphism-permanence](c) makes $g=p
u$ proper. Regard $q$ as a morphism over $X$. Its source is proper over $X$ by the original $f$, and its target is separated over $X$ by properness of $g$. [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated] now makes $q$ proper. On the generic fibre $q_\eta=
u_\eta^{-1}h_\eta$ and $g_\eta=p_\eta
u_\eta$ are isomorphisms. The curves $Y,H,X$ are flat, so their generic opens are schematically dense by step 1. Thus both $q$ and $g$ are $\eta$-modifications. No lifting criterion for a nonexistent map $H	o X$ is being assumed.

source.place: Tags 01WN (finite morphisms proper) and 01W6 (proper source to separated target)

proof.text: The horizontal-curve-models statement, with empty marking, gives finitely many irreducible components for each of the $T$-curves $Y$ and $H$ with smooth generic fibre. Every component meets the generic fibre: on a reduced affine chart, the nonzerodivisor $a$ of step 1 avoids every minimal prime, so every affine generic point lies in $D(a)$. For an affine open $W=\operatorname{Spec}R$ in either normal curve there are therefore finitely many minimal primes. Its local rings are normal domains, so $R$ is a normal ring in the stated localization definition. [lem-weil-pbc-reduced-normal-iff-integrally-closed-total-fractions] writes $R$ as a finite product of normal domains. By the finite affine coproduct-spectrum statement, $W$ is a finite disjoint union of affine normal integral opens. Hence $Y$ and $H$ have open covers by such integral opens, without any Noetherian assumption on $V$.

source.place: Tag 0357 (normal scheme with locally finitely many irreducible components), via Algebra Tag 030C

proof.text: Fix one normal integral affine open $U\subset H$ from step 9 and put $Y_U=q^{-1}U$. The restricted map $q_U:Y_U\to U$ is proper by proper base change. The source $Y_U$ is reduced. Every generic point of a component of $Y_U$ is a generic point of $Y$ lying over $\eta$ by step 9. Since $q_\eta$ is an isomorphism and $U_\eta$ is an open in the integral $U$, these generic points map to the unique generic point $\xi$ of $U$. There is exactly one such point: $q_\eta$ identifies the components of the generic fibres and $U$ meets precisely one of them. Thus $Y_U$ is integral. Moreover $(Y_U)_\xi\simeq\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(\xi)$ by the generic-fibre isomorphism, so its global function algebra is $\kappa(\xi)$. Apply [lem-trf-proper-normal-geometric-connectedness] with base $U$ (not with base $T$): properness, integral normal base, reduced source, the generic-point condition and the generic function-algebra condition have all just been checked. It gives geometrically connected fibres of $q_U$. The opens $U$ cover $H$, proving the geometric connectedness assertion for $q$.

Fix $s\in T$ and a reduced irreducible component $A\subset Y_s$. The maps $q_s$ and $h_s$ are proper by base change, so their scheme-theoretic images on $A$ are closed finite-type $\kappa(s)$-schemes. Let $B$ be the reduced image of $A$ under $q_s$ and $C$ its reduced image under $h_s$. The finite map $\nu_s$ induces a finite surjection $B\to C$: restriction of a finite morphism to a closed subscheme is finite onto its schematic image, and reduction kills nilpotents without changing images. The finite-surjective dimension statement gives $\dim B=\dim C$. Therefore $q$ contracts $A$ if and only if the graph $h$ contracts $A$.

source.place: Tag 00OK (lemma-integral-sub-dim-equal), applied to finite-type fibre images

proof.text: The graph image of the irreducible $A$ is zero-dimensional only if both its projection images are zero-dimensional: a singleton image projects to singletons. Conversely assume $f(A)=\{x\}$ and $u(A)=\{z\}$, which is exactly what zero-dimensional image means here: the image of the generic point of $A$ is a generic point for each image, so any distinct point would give a strict specialization chain in that image. Properness of $f_s|_A$ makes $x$ closed in $X_s$. The Zariski lemma gives finite $\kappa(x)/\kappa(s)$. The closed-fibre $A\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$ is proper, so $A$ is proper over $\kappa(s)$; hence its map to the separated $\mathbf P^1_{\kappa(s)}$ is proper by proper-to-separated and $z$ is closed, again with finite residue extension. The reduced $A$ factors through both residue-field points: the pullback of the respective vanishing ideal has zero germ in every residue field and thus is zero on $A$. Therefore its graph is contained in $\operatorname{Spec}(\kappa(x)\otimes_{\kappa(s)}\kappa(z))$. This algebra is finite-dimensional over $\kappa(s)$, hence has dimension zero (in a finite-dimensional domain multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and therefore surjective). Thus the graph image is zero-dimensional. With step 11 this proves the component criterion in both directions.

source.place: Agent expansion of the graph-contraction sentence in the final paragraph of Proposition 4.4.6 proof, printed p. 33

proof.text: Let $b\in H$ with $\dim Y_b=0$. Properness makes $Y_b$ finite type over $\kappa(b)$. Apply the zero-dimensional closed-subscheme statement to the identity closed immersion $Y_b\hookrightarrow Y_b$; it gives a finite underlying set. [lem-trf-proper-finite-fibre-finite-near] now supplies an open neighbourhood $W\ni b$ such that $q^{-1}W\to W$ is finite. Shrink $W$ inside an integral affine open from step 9. As checked in step 10, $q^{-1}W$ is integral and its map to $W$ induces an isomorphism of function fields. [lem-trf-finite-birational-normal-iso] applies to this finite map with normal integral target $W$ and makes it an isomorphism. Conversely, over an isomorphism neighbourhood every fibre is the spectrum of its residue field and has dimension zero. Thus the locus where $q$ fails to be an isomorphism on any target neighbourhood is exactly $\{b:\dim Y_b>0\}$. The complement is a union of open isomorphism neighbourhoods, and their inverse morphisms agree on overlaps, so $q$ is an isomorphism over that complement. This closed locus is precisely the modification locus. The field-curve isomorphism theorem is not applied to a relative curve over $V$.

source.place: Tags 02UP (lemma-proper-finite-fibre-finite-in-neighbourhood) and 06LH (zero-dimensional algebraic scheme); Morphisms Tag 0AB1 (finite birational over normal)

proof.text: Finally let $U\subset X$ be an open over which $f$ is an isomorphism. Scheme-image restriction identifies $I\times_XU$ with the graph of the actual morphism $u|_{f^{-1}U}$ on $U$. Thus $I\times_XU\simeq U$, a normal scheme. Cover $U$ by normal integral affine opens as in step 9. Above each, $\nu$ is finite birational with integral source, so [lem-trf-finite-birational-normal-iso] makes it an isomorphism. These inverses agree, and $h$ is itself an isomorphism onto this graph. From $\nu q=h$ it follows that $q$ is an isomorphism over $U$, as asserted. The empty curve or empty open has the same argument with empty covers.
